claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi is a single-phase, chemically disordered solid solution.
The starting alloy has only modest local lattice distortion and lacks significant short-range chemical order.
Nearly balanced atomic-size and electronic effects among Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti produce intrinsically weak solid-solution strengthening.
Low atomic-size mismatch and random chemical occupation cause modest dislocation pinning and easy dislocation glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Easy dislocation glide gives the starting alloy favorable plasticity and machinability at the expense of hardness and strength.
Zr has a sufficiently larger atomic radius that an approximately 5 at% addition should increase local lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
A roughly 5 at% Zr addition or slight departure from equimolar composition should promote short-range chemical ordering.
Greater atomic mismatch increases resistance to dislocation motion through enhanced friction or pinning.
Chemical ordering can alter dislocation-mediated deformation and create additional barriers to slip.
Increased lattice distortion and short-range order in modified CoCrFeNiTi should increase hardness and yield strength.
The proposed modification should reduce plastic strain relative to the starting alloy.
The strengthening and ductility tradeoff should persist under quasi-static loading from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C.
The modified alloy should show greater measured lattice strain or local distortion than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
The comparison is intended to isolate local distortion and chemical ordering by using identical thermomechanical processing and similar phase structures.
The hypothesis is limited to minor compositional changes, on the order of 5 at%, that do not produce secondary phases.
Grain size and processing-induced defect structures could govern some of the observed mechanical behavior instead of local lattice effects alone.
Failure of the modified alloy to increase hardness and yield strength is proposed as a falsification result.
Failure to detect an increase in lattice distortion or short-range order is proposed as a falsification result.
